name: The Śvetāmbara canon of forty-five Āgamas

definitions.definition: Eleven Aṅgas, twelve Upāṅgas, ten Prakīrṇakas, six Chedasūtras, four Mūlasūtras and two Cūlikāsūtras (Nandī, Anuyogadvāra), with the Kalpa Sūtra read as part of the Daśāśrutaskandha; the commentarial layers (niryukti, bhāṣya, cūrṇi, ṭīkā) are authoritative with them.

The Sthānakavāsīs accept thirty-two of these: 11 Aṅgas, 12 Upāṅgas, 4 Chedasūtras (Niśītha, Vyavahāra, Bṛhatkalpa, Daśāśrutaskandha), 4 Mūlasūtras (Uttarādhyayana, Daśavaikālika, Nandī, Anuyogadvāra) and the Āvaśyaka; not the Prakīrṇakas, the Mahāniśītha, the Jītakalpa or the Piṇḍa-/Ogha-niryukti.
The Terāpanthīs accept the same thirty-two as the Sthānakavāsīs.
The Digambaras accept none of these as authentic; the original Aṅgas are lost.

relations.note: the two sects' opposed views of what survives

notes: The count of 45 and the grouping are medieval; the Nandī uses the aṅga-praviṣṭa / aṅga-bāhya scheme instead.

definitions.definition: The 'twelve-limbed basket of the gaṇin' composed by the gaṇadharas: Ācārāṅga, Sūtrakṛtāṅga, Sthānāṅga, Samavāyāṅga, Vyākhyāprajñapti (Bhagavatī), Jñātādharmakathā, Upāsakadaśā, Antakṛddaśā, Anuttaraupapātikadaśā, Praśnavyākaraṇa, Vipākaśruta, and the lost Dṛṣṭivāda.

Aupapātika, Rājapraśnīya, Jīvājīvābhigama, Prajñāpanā, Sūryaprajñapti, Jambūdvīpaprajñapti, Candraprajñapti, Nirayāvalikā, Kalpāvataṃsikā, Puṣpikā, Puṣpacūlikā, Vṛṣṇidaśā — each paired with an Aṅga (the order of the 5th–7th varies between lists).
Six: Niśītha, Mahāniśītha, Vyavahāra, Bṛhatkalpa, Daśāśrutaskandha and Jītakalpa (Pañcakalpa in older lists).
Four: Niśītha, Vyavahāra, Bṛhatkalpa, Daśāśrutaskandha.
Uttarādhyayana, Daśavaikālika, Āvaśyaka, and Piṇḍaniryukti or Oghaniryukti.
Uttarādhyayana, Daśavaikālika, Nandī and Anuyogadvāra (with the Āvaśyaka counted separately).

In the usual list: Catuḥśaraṇa, Āturapratyākhyāna, Mahāpratyākhyāna, Bhaktaparijñā, Taṇḍulavaicārika, Saṃstāraka, Gacchācāra, Gaṇividyā, Devendrastava, Maraṇasamādhi; other lists substitute Candravedhyaka, Vīrastava and others.

name: The fourteen Pūrvas

definitions.definition: The 'former' texts contained in the Dṛṣṭivāda: Utpāda, Agrāyaṇīya, Vīryapravāda, Astināstipravāda, Jñānapravāda, Satyapravāda, Ātmapravāda, Karmapravāda, Pratyākhyāna, Vidyānupravāda, Kalyāṇa (Avandhya), Prāṇāvāya, Kriyāviśāla and Lokabindusāra; lost after Bhadrabāhu (in meaning, the last four after him; in text, progressively).
Part of the Agrāyaṇīya survives in the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and part of the Jñānapravāda in the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa.

notes: Names and order recalled with moderate confidence.

name: The five parts of the Dṛṣṭivāda

definitions.definition: Parikarma, sūtra, pūrvagata (the fourteen Pūrvas), anuyoga and cūlikā.

name: The councils (vācanā) of the Jain canon

definitions.definition: Pāṭaliputra (after the twelve-year famine, c. 160 years after the nirvāṇa, with Sthūlabhadra); Mathurā under Skandila and, at the same time, Valabhī under Nāgārjuna (c. 827–840 years after); Valabhī under Devarddhigaṇi (980 or 993 years after, 453 or 466 CE), where the canon was written down and the recensions reconciled.
The Digambaras do not accept these councils as preserving the authentic Aṅgas.

Niryukti (Prakrit verse, ascribed to Bhadrabāhu), bhāṣya (Prakrit verse, e.g. Jinabhadra, Saṅghadāsa), cūrṇi (Prakrit-Sanskrit prose, e.g. Jinadāsa), and ṭīkā or vṛtti (Sanskrit: Haribhadra, Śīlāṅka, Śāntisūri, Abhayadeva, Malayagiri); with the Aṅgas these form the 'five-limbed' (pañcāṅgī) scripture of the Mūrtipūjakas, which the Sthānakavāsīs reject beyond the root texts.

name: The ten niryuktis ascribed to Bhadrabāhu

definitions.definition: On the Āvaśyaka, Daśavaikālika, Uttarādhyayana, Ācārāṅga, Sūtrakṛtāṅga, Daśāśrutaskandha, Bṛhatkalpa, Vyavahāra, Sūryaprajñapti and Ṛṣibhāṣita (the last two lost).

The Digambara arrangement of all scripture: prathamānuyoga (narratives of the great persons: the purāṇas), karaṇānuyoga (cosmology and the mathematics of karma: Tiloyapaṇṇatti, Gommaṭasāra), caraṇānuyoga (conduct: Mūlācāra, Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra) and dravyānuyoga (substances and the self: Kundakunda, the Tattvārthasūtra).

Āryarakṣita is said to have divided the teaching into four anuyogas — caraṇakaraṇa (conduct), dharmakathā (narrative), gaṇita (calculation, cosmology) and dravya (substances) — because pupils could no longer grasp all aspects of every sūtra at once.

name: The loss of the canon (Digambara account)

definitions.definition: The knowledge of the Aṅgas and Pūrvas declined step by step after Mahāvīra — three omniscients (62 years), five śrutakevalins (100), eleven knowers of ten Pūrvas (183), five of the eleven Aṅgas (220), four of the Ācārāṅga (118) — until 683 years after the nirvāṇa no complete Aṅga was known; only portions reached Dharasena and Guṇadhara and were written as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kaṣāyapāhuḍa. The Śvetāmbara Āgamas are therefore not the original scripture.

Gautama, Sudharman (Lohārya) and Jambū (omniscients); Viṣṇu, Nandimitra, Aparājita, Govardhana, Bhadrabāhu (śrutakevalins); eleven daśapūrvins beginning with Viśākha; five knowers of the eleven Aṅgas; four knowers of the Ācārāṅga ending with Lohārya II (names low confidence).

Sudharman, Jambū, Prabhava, Śayyambhava, Yaśobhadra, Sambhūtavijaya and Bhadrabāhu, Sthūlabhadra, Mahāgiri and Suhastin, and their branches down to Devarddhigaṇi, as in the Kalpa Sūtra and Nandī; the gacchas trace their paṭṭāvalīs from it.
The Arhat speaks the meaning (artha); the gaṇadharas compose it as sūtras; the scripture so formed is in meaning beginningless and eternal, re-proclaimed by every Tīrthaṅkara.
The Digambaras add that the Jina's teaching issues as the divine sound (divyadhvani), which the gaṇadharas render.

relations.note: unlike the authorless Veda of the Mīmāṃsakas, Jain scripture has a knowing speaker, the omniscient

name: The schismatics (nihnava)

definitions.definition: Seven (Sthānāṅga) or eight (with the Boṭikas, in the Āvaśyaka commentaries): Jamāli (action in progress is not yet done), Tiṣyagupta (the soul is only its last space-point), Āṣāḍha (agnosticism about who is a true monk), Aśvamitra (momentariness), Gaṅga (two cognitions at once), Rohagupta (three categories), Goṣṭhāmāhila (karma touches but does not bind the soul), and Śivabhūti (nakedness required).

notes: Doctrines of the middle five recalled with low confidence.

name: The debates of the eleven gaṇadharas

definitions.definition: Each of the eleven brāhmaṇas who became Mahāvīra's gaṇadharas held a hidden doubt, resolved by Mahāvīra: whether there is a soul (Indrabhūti), karma (Agnibhūti), a soul other than the body (Vāyubhūti), real elements (Vyakta), rebirth in like form (Sudharman), bondage and liberation (Maṇḍika), gods (Mauryaputra), hell-beings (Akampita), merit and demerit (Acalabhrātṛ), another world (Metārya), nirvāṇa (Prabhāsa).

name: The four doctrines of the rivals (samavasaraṇa)

definitions.definition: All non-Jain teachers fall under kriyāvāda (action has fruit; soul exists), akriyāvāda (denial of action, of soul or of its fruit), ajñānavāda (knowledge is useless or impossible) and vinayavāda (salvation by reverence and discipline alone) — 363 views in the later count (180, 84, 67, 32).

notes: See also U33's treatment of the same scheme (trm:samavasarana-vada).

name: The five grounds of monastic judgment

definitions.definition: Āgama (supernormal knowledge), śruta (scripture), ājñā (instruction), dhāraṇā (retained tradition) and jīta (established practice), used in that order of preference.

name: The twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras of this era

definitions.definition: Ṛṣabha, Ajita, Sambhava, Abhinandana, Sumati, Padmaprabha, Supārśva, Candraprabha, Suvidhi (Puṣpadanta), Śītala, Śreyāṃsa, Vāsupūjya, Vimala, Ananta, Dharma, Śānti, Kunthu, Ara, Malli, Munisuvrata, Nami, Nemi (Ariṣṭanemi), Pārśva and Mahāvīra (Vardhamāna); twenty-four appear in every half-cycle in Bharata and Airāvata, while in Mahāvideha Tīrthaṅkaras are always present.
The nineteenth, Mallī, was a woman.
All were men; they reached nirvāṇa at Aṣṭāpada (Ṛṣabha), Campā (Vāsupūjya), Ūrjayanta (Nemi), Pāvā (Mahāvīra) and Sammeda Śikhara (the other twenty).

Conception (descent into the womb), birth, renunciation, omniscience and nirvāṇa of each Tīrthaṅkara, at each of which the gods come to celebrate — at birth Indra bathes the child on Mount Meru; the events are re-enacted in the consecration of images (pañcakalyāṇaka-pratiṣṭhā).

name: The dreams of a Tīrthaṅkara's mother

definitions.definition: Fourteen: elephant, bull, lion, the anointing of Śrī, a garland, the moon, the sun, a banner, a full vase, a lotus lake, the milk ocean, a celestial palace, a heap of jewels, a smokeless fire.
Sixteen: adding a pair of fish and a lion-throne (and substituting the palace of the nāgas for the heavenly palace in some lists; low confidence on the details).

In each half-cycle: 24 Tīrthaṅkaras, 12 world-emperors (Bharata, Sagara, Maghavā, Sanatkumāra, Śānti, Kunthu, Ara, Subhūma, Mahāpadma, Hariṣeṇa, Jayasena, Brahmadatta), 9 baladevas (the eighth is Rāma, the ninth Balarāma), 9 vāsudevas (Tripṛṣṭha … Lakṣmaṇa, Kṛṣṇa) and 9 prativāsudevas (Aśvagrīva … Rāvaṇa, Jarāsandha).

relations.note: the Jain universal history re-tells figures of the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata (Rāma, Kṛṣṇa) inside its own scheme

definitions.definition: The circular assembly hall created by the gods for the omniscient Jina's preaching, with concentric enclosures in which gods, humans and animals sit in twelve assemblies; the Jina appears to face all four directions.

name: The divine sound of the Jina

definitions.definition: An undifferentiated sound issuing from the Jina without movement of lips, at set times of day, understood by every being in its own speech and rendered into scripture by the gaṇadharas.
The Jina speaks Ardhamāgadhī, which by a supernatural excellence becomes the speech of each listener.

name: The thirty-four excellences of a Jina

definitions.definition: Supernatural features of a Tīrthaṅkara — four from birth (e.g. sweet-smelling, sweatless body; white blood), eleven arising with omniscience (e.g. the voice understood by all, the halo, freedom from famine and disease for many leagues), nineteen produced by the gods (e.g. the wheel of dharma, the parasols, the lion-throne).
Aśoka tree, rain of flowers, divine sound, pair of fly-whisks, lion-throne, halo, divine drum, triple parasol — the attendants of the omniscient Jina shown in his images.

name: The eighteen faults absent in the Jina

definitions.definition: Hunger, thirst, fear, anger, attachment, delusion, anxiety, old age, disease, death, sweat, fatigue, pride, pleasure, wonder, sleep, birth and distress — hence the Jina does not eat.

A different list of eighteen: the five obstructions (to giving, gain, enjoyment, repeated enjoyment and energy), laughter, liking, disliking, fear, disgust, grief, desire, wrong view, ignorance, sleep, non-restraint, attachment and aversion — hunger and thirst are not among them (moderate confidence).

relations.note: the Digambara list excludes the kevalin's eating; the Śvetāmbara list does not

definitions.definition: Bull (Ṛṣabha), elephant, horse, monkey, curlew or ruddy goose, red lotus, svastika, crescent moon, makara, śrīvatsa (or wish-tree), rhinoceros, buffalo, boar, falcon (or porcupine), vajra, deer, goat, nandyāvarta (or fish), water-jar, tortoise, blue lotus, conch, serpent (Pārśva), lion (Mahāvīra) — variants give the Śvetāmbara then the Digambara emblem.

Sixteen (ṣoḍaśa-kāraṇa-bhāvanā): purity of faith, humility, faultless vows, constant knowledge, longing for release, giving and austerity according to strength, the monks' composure and service, devotion to Arhats, teachers, the learned and scripture, the obligatory duties, spreading the path and affection for fellow believers.
Twenty 'places' (vīsa-sthānaka), from devotion to the Arhats to the propagation of the teaching (list from the Jñātādharmakathā and niryukti; low confidence on its items).

name: The twenty living Tīrthaṅkaras of Mahāvideha

definitions.definition: In the Mahāvideha regions, where time does not decline, twenty Tīrthaṅkaras are teaching now, beginning with Sīmandhara; liberation is always possible there, and devotees pray to be reborn there.

name: The ten wonders (accheraga) of this era

definitions.definition: Events that should not happen but did in this descending half-cycle: an attack on a Jina (Gośāla's); the transfer of Mahāvīra's embryo; a woman Tīrthaṅkara (Mallī); a first sermon in which no one took vows; Kṛṣṇa's journey to Amarakaṅkā; the sun and moon coming down in their own vehicles to Mahāvīra; the origin of the Harivaṃśa from a pair of the happy age; Camara's assault on heaven; 108 liberated at once (in Ṛṣabha's time); the worship of the unrestrained.

name: Pārśva's fourfold restraint and Mahāvīra's five vows

definitions.definition: Pārśva taught restraint from violence, falsehood, theft and possessions (chastity being implied in non-possession) and allowed garments; Mahāvīra taught five great vows and nakedness; the Keśin–Gautama dialogue explains the difference by the dispositions of the people of each era, and Pārśva's followers joined Mahāvīra's order.

relations.note: the fourfold restraint was expanded into the five great vows

name: The dispositions of disciples in different eras

definitions.definition: The first Jina's disciples were simple and slow (ṛju-jaḍa), the last Jina's crooked and slow (vakra-jaḍa), the intermediate ones simple and wise (ṛju-prājña); therefore the law is stated as five vows for the first and last, four for the middle ones, and discipline is adapted accordingly.

relations.note: an adaptation of teaching to the capacity of the hearer

definitions.definition: Monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen, together the 'ford' (tīrtha) founded by a Tīrthaṅkara; the Kalpa Sūtra counts Mahāvīra's as 14,000 monks, 36,000 nuns, 159,000 laymen and 318,000 laywomen.

name: The Jain wheel of time (canonical account)

definitions.definition: Time turns without beginning in descending (avasarpiṇī) and ascending (utsarpiṇī) halves of six ages each; at the end of the third age of the descending half the wish-fulfilling trees fail, the patriarchs (kulakara) and then Ṛṣabha teach the arts of civilization, and twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras appear in the third and fourth ages.

notes: Contribution from the canon and purāṇas; the systematic cosmology is U35's.

name: The Jain brāhmaṇa and householder rites

definitions.definition: Bharata made the vow-keeping laity who would not tread on sprouts into brāhmaṇas, gave them the sacred thread as a sign of their vows and the life-cycle rites (kriyā) — a Jain counterpart of the Brahmanical saṃskāras.
The true brāhmaṇa is made by conduct, not birth (Uttarādhyayana 25).

relations.note: both make varṇa depend on conduct or occupation rather than birth alone

name: The true brāhmaṇa (by conduct, not birth)

definitions.definition: Not shaving, the syllable Oṃ, forest-dwelling or bark garments make the śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, sage or ascetic, but equanimity, chastity, knowledge and austerity; by one's acts one becomes a brāhmaṇa or a śūdra.
The true sacrifice is austerity burning karma: austerity the fire, the soul the altar, right exertion the ladle, the body the fuel, restraint the peace-formula (Harikeśa, Uttarādhyayana 12).

relations.note: the Vedic sacrifice re-read as inner discipline
rejects the animal sacrifice in favour of austerity

definitions.definition: Women can reach omniscience and liberation in a female body: the canon lists women among the fifteen kinds of siddhas, Mallī was a woman Tīrthaṅkara, Marudevī was the first liberated of this era, and nuns hold the great vows.
Affirmed with arguments: nothing in a woman opposes the three jewels; the garment is not possession; incapacity for the lowest hell does not imply incapacity for liberation.

Denied: a woman cannot give up clothing, lacks the strongest bodily constitution needed for pure meditation, and her body is a site of the generation of subtle beings; she can reach the fifth stage (a nun is ranked with advanced laity) and may be reborn as a man; canonical 'female siddhas' refers to psychological sex.

relations.note: the Digambara denial rests largely on the requirement of nudity

definitions.definition: The omniscient, while his gross body lasts, takes food; hunger and the other hardships due to feeling-karma occur in him (Tattvārthasūtra 9.11 read literally); Mahāvīra recovered from illness on food brought from Revatī.
Affirmed with arguments by Śākaṭāyana.

Denied: hunger and thirst are among the eighteen faults absent in the Jina; without deluding karma feeling-karma cannot cause hunger; the omniscient's body is sustained without morsel-food; he has no bodily pleasure or pain.
Complete nudity ('the form of the newborn') is required of the fully renounced; clothing, however small, is possession and bars liberation even for a Tīrthaṅkara.

Possession is attachment; clothes and bowls kept for restraint are not possessions. The Ācārāṅga allows three, two, one or no garments; Mahāvīra went naked, but the naked Jinakalpa mode lapsed after Jambū, and the Keśin–Gautama dialogue shows the outward sign is secondary to knowledge, faith and conduct.
Nudity is the normal sign, but a garment may be kept by exception, and at death may be given up; women and those with just cause are not excluded from liberation.

name: The two modes of mendicant life

definitions.definition: The Jinakalpa — solitary, naked or nearly equipment-less, of extreme rigour, for those of the strongest constitution and scriptural learning — and the Sthavirakalpa — life in the community with minimal clothing and equipment; the first ended after Jambū, the second is the valid mode now.
The Digambaras recognize no such lapse: nudity remains the only mode of full renunciation.

After Jambū, the last omniscient, ten things ceased in Bharata: mind-reading knowledge, the highest clairvoyance, certain supernormal powers, the conveyance body, the two ladders of karmic subsidence and destruction, the Jinakalpa, the three highest forms of conduct, omniscience and liberation (list low confidence).

Sex is twofold: the bodily marks and the rise of the karma of sexual desire, which need not coincide; liberation may be reached with any psychological sex but only with the male body — the Digambara key to reading canonical passages about women among the liberated.
Śvetāmbaras accept the distinction but hold that liberation is possible with the female body.

Consecrated images of the Jinas are worshipped by laity with material offerings and by all with inner worship; the image is the Jina 'placed' (sthāpanā) and a support for recalling his qualities, not a grace-giver; the canon shows gods and Draupadī worshipping Jina images.
Image worship is practised (the Bīsapantha with fresh offerings, the Terāpantha with dry, non-living offerings only).
Rejected: the thirty-two Āgamas contain no injunction to it, and worship with water, flowers and lamps harms living beings; devotion is to the Jina's qualities and to living mendicants.
Rejected likewise.
Rejected; the shrines keep scriptures instead of images.

Ācārya Bhikṣu distinguished worldly (laukika) duties — social help, saving bodily life, charity to the unrestrained — from spiritual (lokottara) dharma, which alone stops karmic inflow; the first may be socially good but is not dharma in the strict sense.
Opponents hold that compassion that saves life (jīva-rakṣā) and giving are themselves religious merit and part of dharma.

name: The divisions of the Jain community

definitions.definition: The main division into Śvetāmbara and Digambara (with the extinct Yāpanīya between them), turning on monastic nudity, women's liberation, the omniscient's eating, the canon and details of Mahāvīra's life; within the Śvetāmbaras, the image-worshipping Mūrtipūjakas and the aniconic Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs; within the Digambaras, the Bīsapantha, Terāpantha and Tāraṇapantha.
The Digambaras arose from Śivabhūti's Boṭika schism, 609 years after the nirvāṇa.
The Śvetāmbaras arose from monks who stayed in the north during Bhadrabāhu's famine and adopted clothing.

members: Digambara (Bīsapantha, Terāpantha, Tāraṇapantha, Kānjī Svāmī movement)

definitions.definition: The medieval and modern monastic lineages — Tapā (1228), Kharatara (1024), Añcala, Pārśvacandra, Tristuti, Upakeśa and others — each with its line of ācāryas (paṭṭāvalī), ritual details and festival calendar.

In early medieval western India many monks lived permanently in temples, handling their property; Haribhadra condemned this, and Jineśvara's debate at Aṇahilapāṭaka (1024) won recognition for monks living in lodgings (vasati), the origin of the Kharatara reform.

From about the 13th c., clothed clerics (bhaṭṭārakas) presided over Digambara seats, temples, libraries and rites, filling the gap left by the near-absence of naked monks; the Bīsapantha accepts them, the Terāpantha rejected them; seats survive in the south (Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, Mūḍabidri, Humcha).

The Mūla Saṅgha (Kundakundānvaya, with the Nandi, Sena, Deva and Siṃha gaṇas and later the Balātkāra gaṇa), and the Kāṣṭhā, Drāviḍa and Māthura saṅghas — the latter three condemned as deviant in Devasena's Darśanasāra, later accepted as Digambara branches; the Yāpanīya was a separate order.

Bīsapantha (older temple practice, bhaṭṭārakas, fresh offerings, attendant deities), Terāpantha (17th-c. lay reform: no bhaṭṭārakas, dry offerings, no attendant deities), Tāraṇapantha (aniconic; scriptures in shrines), Totāpantha (a mixed practice; low confidence), and in recent times the Kānjī Svāmī movement.

name: The single-ācārya discipline of the Terāpanth

definitions.definition: One ācārya initiates all monks and nuns, who keep no personal disciples; he appoints his successor; the order lives by a written code (maryādā) renewed every year at the Maryādā Mahotsava.

name: The twenty-eight root qualities of the Digambara monk

definitions.definition: Five great vows, five carefulnesses, restraint of the five senses, six obligatory duties, and seven special rules — plucking the hair, nakedness, not bathing, sleeping on the ground, not cleaning the teeth, eating standing, eating once a day.

name: The ten points of monastic conduct (sāmācārī)

definitions.definition: Formal courtesies and procedures of the monk toward teacher and fellow monks (announcing going out and returning, asking leave, inviting others to share alms, and the like) and the division of day and night into study, meditation, alms and sleep.

notes: The ten items are not listed here individually (not recalled with confidence).

name: The six classes of living beings

definitions.definition: Earth-bodied, water-bodied, fire-bodied, wind-bodied and plant-bodied beings (one-sensed) and mobile beings (two- to five-sensed); non-harm extends to all six in thought, word and deed.
Human birth, hearing the dharma, faith in it, and energy in self-restraint are hard to obtain (Uttarādhyayana 3.1); hence 'wake up — the nights do not return'.

name: Death against one's will and death with one's will

definitions.definition: The ignorant die unwillingly, clinging and afraid; the wise and restrained die willingly and composed — the root of the later classification of deaths.

Death of the wise-among-the-wise (the omniscient), of the wise (the renunciant), of the wise-ignorant (the vowed layperson), of the ignorant (right faith without vows) and of the ignorant-among-the-ignorant (wrong faith).
The Ācārāṅga's three forms of the wise monk's death and the Prakīrṇakas on the preparation of the dying (restricted theme: the texts' conditions only).
Of right faith, right knowledge, right conduct and austerity, brought to completion at the end of life.

relations.note: the three jewels with austerity added (as in Uttarādhyayana 28)

name: The fifteen kinds of liberated beings

definitions.definition: Liberated as Tīrthaṅkara or not; during or outside a Tīrthaṅkara's ford; self-enlightened, enlightened by an outer cause (pratyekabuddha) or taught; in female, male or neuter body; in Jain garb, other garb or as householder; singly or together.
Digambaras read the categories of sex and garb retrospectively or as psychological sex, not as liberation from a female or clothed body.
Upakrama (introduction), nikṣepa (placement of meanings), anugama (following the text) and naya (standpoints) — the method of the Anuyogadvāra.

Destiny, sense, body-type, activity, sex, passion, knowledge, restraint, perception, leśyā, capacity for liberation, right faith, rationality, nourishment — the grid through which the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama examines souls in the fourteen guṇasthānas.
The soul abiding in its own faith, knowledge and conduct is sva-samaya; identified with karmic matter and its states it is para-samaya; the whole path is the return from the second to the first.

name: Pure, good and bad activity of consciousness

definitions.definition: Bad activity (aśubhopayoga: passion, violence) binds demerit; good activity (śubhopayoga: devotion, vows, compassion) binds merit — a golden fetter; pure activity (śuddhopayoga: abiding in the self as equanimity) alone liberates.
The intention to harm is itself violence and bears its fruit even if no being is actually killed — as King Yaśodhara and his mother suffered many animal births for sacrificing a cock of flour.

Beyond description: no sound, reasoning or mind reaches it; not long or short, of no colour, not female, male or neuter; it knows and perceives; formless being (Ācārāṅga 1.5.6); the liberated rise to the summit of the world, where the medium of motion ends, and there enjoy unobstructed happiness (Aupapātika, Uttarādhyayana 36).

Mahāvīra's attainment: 'infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete and full' knowledge and perception, arising in pure meditation after the destruction of the obscuring, deluding and obstructing karmas; 'who knows one knows all'.

The Ācārāṅga's starting point: one who knows 'my soul is reborn' believes in soul, world, karma and action; the soul is eternal as substance and non-eternal as modes; the self is the doer and undoer of its own happiness and suffering, its own friend and foe.

The pure, eternal law proclaimed by all Arhats: no being is to be killed, ruled, enslaved, tormented or driven away; all beings love life; 'you are the one you intend to kill'; the essence of wisdom is not to kill anything.

Arhats, Siddhas, Ācāryas, Upādhyāyas and Sādhus, saluted in the Namaskāra that opens the Bhagavatī (Śvetāmbara) and the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama (Digambara); the salutation is to qualities and ranks, not to named individuals.
Eleven of them (those due to feeling-karma, including hunger and thirst) actually occur in the omniscient; 'nakedness' may be borne as scanty clothing.
In the omniscient the eleven are only figurative; 'nakedness' means complete nudity.

The standpoint of ultimate reality (niścaya), the 'real', shows the soul as pure knower beyond all stages and distinctions; the conventional standpoint (vyavahāra), the 'unreal', speaks of knowledge, faith, conduct, bondage and stages and is indispensable for teaching those at the lower stage, as one must speak to a foreigner in his language.
Ṭoḍarmal warns against both one-sided errors — clinging to niścaya talk while neglecting conduct, and clinging to vyavahāra rites without knowing the self.

relations.note: comparable use of an ultimate and a conventional level of description
